LET’S GO. I reviewed the John Saro triage call, and your read is correct: **John is a legitimate fit, the opportunity is bigger than memberships, and the triage call made the fit sound smaller and less certain than it actually is.** The good news is he stayed engaged, disclosed meaningful business information, and booked the second conversation. This is recoverable. fileciteturn1file0

## Step 1 — Score It

Because this was a **triage call rather than the full sales presentation**, I am scoring what was actually observable. I am not penalizing her heavily for not presenting price or handling a formal price objection that never occurred.

| Domain | Statement | Score |
|---|---|---:|
| **Authority & Presence** | 1. Certainty at Open | 2 — 🔻 Weak |
| | 2. Credentialing Without Over-Explaining | 2 — 🔻 Weak |
| | 3. Certainty Transfers to Prospect | 3 — ⚠ Inconsistent |
| | 4. Command of the Conversation | 2 — 🔻 Weak |
| **Domain Average** | | **2.25/5** |
| **Clarity & Plan Presentation** | 5. Simple Recommendation, Not a Menu | 2 — 🔻 Weak |
| | 6. Transformation First, Process Second | 2 — 🔻 Weak |
| | 7. Minimalism / No Over-Explaining | 1 — ❌ Missing |
| | 8. Next Step Is Crystal Clear | 4 — ⚡ Solid |
| **Domain Average** | | **2.25/5** |
| **Urgency & Decision Guidance** | 9. The Ask | 3 — ⚠ Inconsistent |
| | 10. Staying in the Conversation | 4 — ⚡ Solid |
| | 11. Urgency Aligned to Their Goals | 2 — 🔻 Weak |
| | 12. Managing Emotional / Conversational Energy | 2 — 🔻 Weak |
| **Domain Average** | | **2.75/5** |
| **Pricing & Objection Handling** | 13. Pricing Confidence | 3 — ⚠ Not fully tested |
| | 14. No Pre-Justification | 3 — ⚠ Not fully tested |
| | 15. Deep Objection Exploration | 3 — ⚠ Not fully tested |
| | 16. Return to the Decision | 3 — ⚠ Not fully tested |
| **Domain Average** | | **3.0/5** |

**Total: 41/80**

The biggest issue was not that she “failed to sell” on a triage call. **She failed to diagnose cleanly enough to make the second call easy.** She had a 20-minute qualification call and spent too much of it explaining, self-disclosing, and narrating what she normally would have asked instead of simply asking the questions.

## 🟢 What You Did Well

**1. She identified that both John and his partner are decision-makers.** She asked, *“So right now it’s you and your business partner that are the decision makers, right?”* and John confirmed yes. That is important information, and it means the second call should not become a full proposal and close without the partner present. fileciteturn1file10

**2. She uncovered a very strong expansion opportunity.** John is not thinking about one struggling location. He opened Scottsdale, has already signed a lease for Albuquerque with an October opening, and explicitly said the goal is to expand into additional locations. fileciteturn1file6 That makes the conversation much bigger than “help us build a membership.”

**3. She eventually found the immediate entry point.** John said they are *“literally putting our memberships together as we speak.”* That is the urgent problem. fileciteturn1file8 He is not shopping for vague consulting. He wants a membership model that works now and can eventually be replicated across locations.

## 🔴 Top 3 Conversion Killers

### 1. She incorrectly narrowed your niche and created unnecessary disqualification energy

The line was:

> *“We specialize in medical spas. We don’t do anything else… We only do medical spas.”* fileciteturn1file5

That is factually too narrow based on what you actually do. **You work exclusively with wellness and aesthetic practices.** John operates a weight-loss and wellness practice with GLPs, peptides, body contouring, aesthetics, and future multi-location ambitions. He is not outside the niche. **He is squarely inside it.**

Worse, she had already framed the call with:

> *“Normally this is just a call to see if you are our target audience. If we want to work with you… There’s some people that we don’t work with.”* fileciteturn1file6

Selective positioning is good. But you cannot combine exclusivity with an inaccurate definition of whom you serve. That creates confusion when the prospect is actually a strong fit.

**Word-for-word replacement:**

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="68421"}
“John, just so I’m clear on this because I want to correct something from our earlier conversation: we are exclusive to wellness and aesthetic practices. That includes businesses built around medical weight loss, GLPs, peptides, longevity, body contouring, aesthetics, memberships, and packages. We are not a generalist company working across a dozen unrelated industries. Your model is absolutely within the world we specialize in.”
:::

### 2. She told him what she *would have asked* instead of diagnosing him

This was the clearest breakdown:

> *“Normally I have a list of questions like, you know, how fast you guys follow up, but actually…”* fileciteturn1file10

And earlier:

> *“Normally this call goes like… they’ve been in business for a year, two, three or four or five…”* fileciteturn1file12

No. **Do not narrate the script. Run the script.**

The fact that he opened yesterday does not eliminate diagnosis. It changes the diagnosis. She still needed to uncover:

- What is the actual membership vision?
- What do they want membership revenue to become?
- What is the average patient value target?
- What are the membership tiers or concepts currently being considered?
- What is the conversion process from lead → consult → package → membership?
- What is the staff expected to sell?
- Who owns KPIs?
- What does success look like in 90 days?
- What must be proven in Scottsdale before Albuquerque opens?
- How many locations do they ultimately want?
- What is the eventual exit or acquisition vision?

John handed her a massive clue when he said his goal is to expand and open other locations. fileciteturn1file1 Instead of drilling into the economics and operational requirements of that vision, the call repeatedly moved into explanation.

**Word-for-word replacement for the second call:**

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="31746"}
“John, I know the immediate reason you came to us was memberships, and we’re going to get very specific about that today. Before I recommend anything, though, I need to understand the business you and your partner are actually trying to build. Scottsdale is location one, Albuquerque is already coming, and you’ve told me the larger goal is expansion. So I want to understand what has to be true operationally, financially, and from a membership standpoint for you to feel confident replicating this model. Let me ask you a few direct questions.”
:::

Then **ask the questions and shut up.**

### 3. She feature-dumped the entire backend before establishing what he actually needed

The line was:

> *“We train the sales staff. If you need sales staff, we provide that. We implement the systems. We have 15 playbooks. We have a consultant that looks at, you know, your revenue leaks. We have a market blueprint. We have a marketing leg, we have a tech leg…”* fileciteturn1file2

That is exactly where the conversation became about **everything you do** rather than **what John gets**.

He had already told her he has GHL, AI, multiple marketing agencies, immediate lead follow-up, and sales-experienced staff. fileciteturn1file14 So listing more systems, tech, and backend capabilities risks sounding duplicative.

The better frame is:

**“You have pieces. We determine whether those pieces are actually building one scalable economic model.”**

The recommendation should be the **Premium Growth Package**, because the problem is bigger than designing a membership. But the package needs to be sold through his desired outcome:

- build the right membership architecture now;
- create predictable recurring revenue;
- ensure staff can sell memberships, packages, GLP/peptide programs, laser and longevity offers;
- establish the KPIs needed to know whether Scottsdale is actually scalable;
- diagnose the Scottsdale market and competitive position;
- audit current marketing rather than blindly replacing it;
- if appropriate, focus your marketing execution exclusively on memberships;
- create a model that can be replicated into Albuquerque and future locations;
- build toward multi-location scale and eventual acquisition readiness.

**Word-for-word replacement:**

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="92503"}
“Based on what you’ve told me, I would not recommend treating this as a standalone ‘build us a membership’ project. You’re opening location one, Albuquerque is already coming, you have multiple agencies generating demand, and you need to know that the model you build in Scottsdale can actually be replicated.

Our recommendation is the Premium Growth Package. We start by diagnosing the market and the business model so we know exactly where the opportunity is. Then we build the membership and package strategy around the services you actually want to grow. We audit what your current marketing is doing, and if the right strategy is to focus our marketing execution exclusively on memberships, we can do that. We do not have to come in and blindly replace everything that is already working.

Then we make sure the backend can support the growth. That means your staff knows how to sell memberships and packages, how to position GLPs and peptides appropriately within the offer structure, how to sell higher-value services and longevity programs, and how to track the KPIs that tell you whether this location is ready to scale.

The goal is not just to launch a membership. The goal is to build a recurring-revenue model in Scottsdale that you can confidently take into Albuquerque and every location after that.”
:::

## 🎯 The One Thing Drill

**Question. Answer. Follow-up. Do not teach until the diagnosis is complete.**

For the first **30–40 minutes of the one-hour call**, Arlene’s job is not to explain Luxora. Her job is to understand the business deeply enough that the recommendation feels inevitable.

She should keep this written in front of her:

**“Do not tell them what we do until I can explain, in their words, what they need.”**

For this second call, I would run it approximately like this:

**First 5 minutes:** reset the frame, correct the niche positioning, confirm both decision-makers are present, and establish that this is a 60-minute working session designed to reach a decision if there is a fit.

**Next 30–35 minutes:** diagnose. Membership vision, revenue goals, economics, service mix, current marketing, current conversion, team capability, KPI tracking, Scottsdale success criteria, Albuquerque timeline, future location strategy, and what would make this engagement worth the investment.

**Next 10–15 minutes:** summarize the gap and prescribe **one recommendation: Premium Growth Package.** Do not give them a menu. Do not lead with 15 playbooks, CRM, AI, or a list of deliverables.

**Final 10–15 minutes:** investment, questions, objection handling, and decision.

One more thing: **the partner needs to be there.** John already confirmed they are joint decision-makers. fileciteturn1file10 The first call ended with the idea that the partner could simply listen to the recording afterward. fileciteturn1file15 That is not the standard for a true decision call. If the partner cannot attend, she should not run a full close as though the decision can be made in the room.

The opportunity here is strong. John has sales sophistication, meaningful ad spend, a team, multiple service lines, a second location already underway, and a stated interest in memberships. fileciteturn1file9 **Do not sell him more “stuff.” Sell him the infrastructure that turns Scottsdale into the model he can replicate.**

Want me to build Arlene a **word-for-word one-hour discovery call script for John and his partner**, including the exact diagnostic questions, Premium Growth Package presentation, and likely objection branches?

On this triage call that was supposed to last 20 minutes, she told the prospective client that we basically don't work with people like him. We only work with med spas. We actually work with health and wellness and aesthetic practices. She then continued telling him what we would have been asking instead of just asking him the fucking questions. And then she rambled on telling him every single thing that we do in the background instead of sticking to the script. She now has a second discovery call in an hour and a half, and that call is an hour long, not 30 minutes. And she has to have his partner on the phone with them so that they can make an executive decision. Please evaluate the transcript and put my notes in there. He obviously just wants help with memberships, so we're going to have to make sure that we can a la carte that for him if he does not want diagnostic marketing and the back end. But with that said, that's something we don't do. So we need to offer him the entire premium growth package, which includes a market diagnosis of his entire area, and we can do that for all his new and up-and-coming locations as well. And we also can go ahead and edit, audit, whatever his marketing, and run that exclusively for memberships only if that's the avenue that he'd like to do, but we can also help with other marketing. We are exclusive to wellness and aesthetic practices, so we are not some one-off company that has a bunch of niches. And then the retention in the back, we teach all staff members how to sell memberships packages, laser ROIs, longevity arms. We're very familiar with peptides and how to advertise and sell those while incorporating them into memberships and packages. We also are really good with KPIs and scaling locations to multiple locations as well as getting acquired at some point.
